title: Amazon's Deadly Miami Crash: Cargo Aviation's Safety Blind Spot
summary: A Prime Air-branded Boeing 767 freighter overran the runway in Miami and killed at least five people, and this week we go deep on why cargo aviation operates under a completely different safety rulebook than the passenger airlines you fly. We trace the eerie parallels to the 2019 Atlas Air crash, explain why cargo pilots are exempt from fatigue rules that apply to everyone else, and ask whether Amazon's breakneck expansion is outrunning its safety culture.

topic.topic: Amazon Prime Air 767 crash in Miami kills at least 5 people, marking a critical safety moment for the rapidly expanding cargo airline industry.
topic.why: This is the week's most consequential story because it combines immediate fatality, regulatory implications for a major cargo operator, and broader questions about safety oversight as Amazon aggressively scales its logistics network. Multiple sources covered it, it will dominate aviation safety discussions for months, and it directly impacts how regulators approach cargo operations.
key_facts: Amazon Prime Air Boeing 767-300F overran the runway at Miami International Airport on September 7, 2026, bursting through a fence into a parking lot and catching fire
At least 5 people confirmed dead in the crash
Amazon Prime Air is rapidly expanding its cargo fleet to compete with FedEx and UPS, making this a critical test of oversight during rapid growth
Runway overrun accidents are typically preventable through better procedures, training, or equipment — suggesting systemic rather than random failure
This occurs amid broader cargo airline growth and minimal media scrutiny compared to passenger airlines
